questions.q: Per this lesson, why is documentation rot better understood as a structural problem rather than a sign of team indiscipline?
options: Because nothing in a typical change process automatically updates documentation when the system changes, so without a deliberate counter-process, rot is simply the default outcome of ordinary, legitimate change
Because Salesforce causes documentation to decay automatically over time regardless of what teams do
Because documentation rot only happens to teams that never write documentation in the first place
Because rot is caused exclusively by malicious tampering with documents
questions.explain: Rot isn't evidence of carelessness — it's the predictable result of a change process that doesn't automatically propagate to documentation, which is exactly why a deliberate review process is needed to counter it.

questions.q: According to this lesson's review checklist, what should happen to an ADR whose decision the team has since reversed?
options: The original ADR's Decision section should be edited to reflect the new direction
The ADR's status should be updated to 'Superseded by ADR-0XX,' per the immutable-log convention, rather than being left as a silently stale 'Accepted'
The ADR should be deleted since it's no longer accurate
Nothing — ADRs never need their status updated after being written
questions.explain: This follows Lesson 6's immutable-log convention: the original ADR's content stays as written, but its status should be updated to show it has been superseded, rather than quietly leaving a reversed decision marked 'Accepted.'

questions.q: Why does this lesson reject 'whoever has time' as a real ownership model for documentation review?
options: Because it is technically against Salesforce's terms of service
Because only a Certified Technical Architect is legally allowed to review documentation
Because it means review happens inconsistently or not at all, which is exactly how rot accumulates unchecked — review needs to be tied to a trigger, not to spare time
Because documentation review should never be anyone's explicit responsibility
questions.explain: Without a defined trigger, review happens only opportunistically, which doesn't reliably catch rot — the lesson recommends tying review to concrete triggers (release or calendar) instead.

questions.q: What is the difference between 'release-triggered review' and 'scheduled periodic review,' per this lesson?
options: They are the same thing described with different names
Release-triggered review only applies to security documentation; scheduled review only applies to integration documentation
Scheduled periodic review replaces the need for any release-triggered review

Release-triggered review reviews documentation sections affected by a specific release as part of its checklist; scheduled periodic review happens on a calendar cadence independent of releases, to catch rot from small changes nobody flagged
questions.explain: The two triggers catch different kinds of rot: release-triggered review catches documentation gaps tied to a specific deployed change, while scheduled periodic review catches the slow accumulation of small, undocumented changes between releases.

questions.q: How does this lesson connect regular documentation review to the Salesforce CTA Review Board?
options: It argues that a candidate presenting a design built on documentation that doesn't match reality faces, compressed into one high-stakes session, exactly the mismatch a panel's questions will surface — the same review discipline practiced on real projects is what lets an architect defend a design that still matches what they actually built
It claims the Review Board does not care whether documentation matches reality
It claims the Review Board reviews only diagrams submitted in advance, never live reasoning
It states that documentation review is unrelated to CTA preparation
questions.explain: A panel's pointed questions will quickly surface any mismatch between a presented design and the candidate's actual reasoning — the same regular-review discipline that prevents rot on real projects is what keeps an architect's design defensible under that kind of scrutiny.
